headlines.title: Fire at Berkeley police station prompts evacuation
headlines.description: A small fire at the Berkeley police station has forced officers to evacuate. The police department said 911 calls were being transferred to the Alameda County Dispatch Center. Berkeley police say officers will continue to respond to emergency calls. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: Proposed new name for San Francisco's Cesar Chavez Street sparks debate
headlines.description: Months ago, San Francisco decided to strip Cesar Chavez name off a Mission District street in the wake of accusations of sexual assault and misconduct by the famed labor leader. Since then, the debate has raged about what name the street should carry now. The street used to be called Army Street but was renamed in 1995 to honor labor leader Cesar Chavez. This week, a new name has been proposed: “Las Campesinas”. Some residents say they appreciate the effort by the city to move quickly. “I think that it’s good and I’m actually surprised, pleasantly surprised that they’re attending to it so quickly after the news broke,” resident Dina Saadh said. In April, several firsthand accounts of sexual misconduct by Chavez were published by the New York Times. Among the accusers is co-founder of the United Farm Workers Dolores Huerta. San Jose Mar 24 Agriculture Mar 22 news Mar 18 Almost immediately after those accounts, San Francisco and other cities announced efforts to remove his name from streets and other landmarks. During Tuesday’s Board of Supervisor’s regular meeting, Supervisor Jackie Fielder announced the name that has been selected after a month’s long process. “Today we advance the name ‘Las Campesinas’. When translated, this means women farm workers,” Fielder said. Word has already got out about the name, but not everyone is happy with the final recommendation. A petition has been circulating through Mission neighborhood businesses with more than 150 signatures, voicing concerns about people’s ability to spell the new name or postal workers and emergency responders being able to easily communicate “Las Campesinas” and another finalist name that was considered. Some say it should revert to its old name, Army Street. San Francisco assessor-recorder Joaquin Torres helped steward this renaming process. “We had a very substantive conversation with them and many people about the principal and values that were important to them, and all of them have been considered in the final name of ‘Las Campesinas’,” Torres said. If the board approves the name, it will be submitted to the Department of Public Works to determine the cost of making the necessary changes, including new signs, re-stamped sidewalks and even new transit maps.

headlines.title: San Jose-based eBay to slash 1,000 jobs
headlines.description: San Jose-based eBay is cutting more jobs. The company confirmed Wednesday it will be laying off about 1,000 employees, or 9% of its workforce. eBay declined to say exactly who is impacted by the layoffs or which locations the cuts will come from. Some of those questions could be addressed when eBay releases its third quarter financial report in a week. In a statement to NBC Bay Area, eBay said, “…this step was taken to ensure we continue to operate from a position of strength by aligning our teams and resources with our top strategic priorities.” eBay made its mark as a massive online auction marketplace, but lately it’s been refining its focus to a place for more upscale merchandise. Its last financial report showed quarterly revenue of over $3 billion and a $552 million profit. But the company has been systematically laying off large numbers of employees – about 500 in February 2023, another 1,000 or so in January 2024, and another 800 this past February. Creative Strategies analyst Tim Bajarin said the cuts are all about the AI effect. “AI could do so many of the jobs, especially administration jobs,” he said. “While this is not good news for those who’ve lost their jobs, I’m afraid that this is a part of ongoing strategies with a lot of companies.” San Jose State University Strategic Management Professor Robert Chapman Wood said AI has created an interesting dilemma in Silicon Valley. “The thing that is part of a larger issue is what are we doing with this wild new technology?” he said. “It hasn’t yet produced the kind of jobs boom that earlier technologies have produced, and it hasn’t produced the value for the customer that earlier technologies have produced.”

headlines.title: Last call for San Francisco Chinatown's oldest bar, Red's Place
headlines.description: Red’s Place is known as the “Cheers of Chinatown,” serving up memories that span generations. The neighborhood bar at Jackson Street and Grant Avenue is where locals know your name and tourists come from all over the world. Jerry Chan has run Red’s for almost 20 years – on top of his day job. The bar is set to close its doors as early as the end of October. “Ideally it would be the 31st because of the end of the month,” Chan said. “We’re for sure gonna be done by mid-November.” Chan said he received a letter from the insurance company in early October. “The cost of running an operation, it’s getting too expensive,” Chan said. “But more importantly, our insurance is up. So, sadly, we have to close the door. The insurance company that we go through is forcing us to make mandatory upgrades and that goes from plumbing to structural fixes. It costs a lot, and it’s beyond our means.” Growing up in Chinatown, Chan’s parents bought Red’s Place in 1990. In 2010, he took over. “My mom was ill,” Chan said. “She tapped on my shoulder. She asked me, ‘Hey, do you want to sell the bar or do you wanna run it?’ I told her straight up, ‘Let me run it.’ Ever since then, Red’s has been thriving for the last 16 years.” For decades, Red’s has been famously known as the place to be for Lunar New Year fireworks and festivities. “It goes back to when I was a little boy,” Chan said. “There would be a gathering. Not as crazy as it is this day. Back then it was just basically the community getting together.” Chan said he will save Red’s furniture and signage, but he didn’t say what he’ll do with it. But the Red’s that the city and Chinatown has known for the past decades will soon be no more. Chan noted he does have a day job. He said he’s focusing on himself next, and he might even take a vacation.
headlines.source: Christine Ni, Alex Bozovic and Janelle Wang

headlines.title: Former Oakland hotel workers reach $600K wage theft settlement
headlines.description: After a six-year battle, former Oakland hotel workers are set to receive money owed to them as part of one of the largest wage theft settlements in Oakland. Former Radisson workers joined city leaders and supporters at Oakland City Hall on Wednesday to announce the $600,000 settlement. Under the settlement, 128 former Radisson hotel workers will receive more than $500,000 in unpaid wages and interest. The remaining $100,000 will go toward legal fees. The agreement is between the city of Oakland’s Department of Workplace and Employment Standards and the company that owned the now-closed Radisson Hotel near Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport. The case dates back to 2020, when the East Bay Alliance for a Sustainable Economy, known as EBASE, helped workers file complaints alleging wage theft. Workers reported working long hours without pay, among other alleged labor violations. “With the violation of wage theft came the dehumanization of what it means to be a worker,” EBASE Executive Director Saabir Lockett said. “This is the win about the dignity and honor of standing up, that all work matters and all work has dignity. No matter what you do, you have the right to be treated as a human being and paid fair wages.” The settlement is the largest in the history of the Oakland Department of Workplace and Employment Standards. NBC Bay Area reached out to the hotel owner for comment but has not yet heard back. The former workers are still waiting for the money to reach their bank accounts because the settlement terms are still being workout out.

headlines.title: Child's death in San Jose under investigation
headlines.description: An investigation was launched Tuesday after a child died in San Jose, according to police. Officers responded at about 1:40 p.m. to the 2500 block of Fontaine Road to investigate a report of an unresponsive child, police said. First responders tried to save the child, but the child was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police. Additional information wasn’t immediately known. “As with all major injury or death investigations involving a child, the San José Police Department is conducting an investigation per Santa Clara County protocol and is working closely with the SCC District Attorney’s Office,” police said in a statement. “Investigations into child deaths are highly detailed processes that require extensive evidence collection and thorough follow-up to determine the cause and manner of death.” Police said the investigation is active and ongoing.

headlines.title: 7 students arrested after fight at Santa Rosa high school
headlines.description: Seven students were arrested after a fight at a Santa Rosa high school prompted a campus lockdown Tuesday, with police saying a 15-year-old student displayed a knife and tried to approach another student. Santa Rosa police said they responded to Montgomery High School at 1250 Hahman Drive at about 1:10 p.m. after receiving multiple reports of a physical altercation involving students. Initial reports indicated a knife had been displayed, and some unconfirmed information suggested a firearm might also be involved. Sixteen officers responded as the campus was placed on lockdown while police searched the area, identified students and reviewed video footage. Initial information suggested the fight might be gang-related, police said. Investigators determined that a 15-year-old male student brandished a knife and aggressively advanced toward another student. A school employee stepped between them, preventing the student from advancing further. The student fled before officers arrived. Police found the student hiding behind a residence across the street on Rock Creek Drive. A large knife with a 4-inch fixed blade, believed to have been used, was recovered nearby. Several students had minor injuries and were treated at the scene. One student was taken to a hospital for injuries to the face and hand. Despite the initial reports, police found no firearm. They said they have no evidence that a gun was involved. After officers searched the campus and determined there was no ongoing threat, the lockdown was lifted shortly after 1:55 p.m. Middle school students were released to parents and guardians first, followed by high school students, with officers assisting in the process. All seven students were arrested on suspicion of battery on school grounds. They included a 14-year-old boy, three 15-year-old boys and three 16-year-old boys. One of the 15-year-olds, whom police identified as the student who possessed the knife, was also arrested on suspicion of brandishing a weapon and possessing a weapon on school grounds. Police withheld the students’ names because they are juveniles. Anyone with information about this case can contact the Santa Rosa Police Department’s Gang Crimes Team at 707-543-4021 or submit an anonymous tip at srcity.org/CrimeTips.

headlines.title: East Bay cities move to pause new AI data centers
headlines.description: East Bay cities are taking action on new AI data centers, with Hayward becoming the latest to approve a temporary moratorium on their development. The Hayward City Council approved a 45-day moratorium on the development of new AI data centers Tuesday night. The moratoriums come amid concerns that the large computing facilities are too noisy and strain the electrical grid and water systems. The city says the next month and a half will serve as a timeout for staff to monitor and analyze the impacts of the four AI data centers already in operation. Staff will also assess whether it is wise to approve two new 99-megawatt data centers proposed for the area of Arden Road and Corporate Avenue. The moratorium could be extended for two years. In Richmond Tuesday night, the City Council voted to extend its current moratorium for more than 22 months. During public comment, Richmond resident Toronto Abbott expressed concerns about data centers. “We’re on the cusp of a really terrifying era,” Abbott said. “And it’s not just that the change is different and new.” Abbott said he believes the wealth and power coming from data centers will not benefit residents and expressed concerns about the impact on jobs. On Monday, the Pittsburg City Council directed staff to draft a 45-day moratorium on AI data centers in the city. The Pittsburg City Council will consider that moratorium next Monday.

headlines.title: Man dies after shooting in Oakland
headlines.description: A man died after a shooting in Oakland early Wednesday morning, according to police. Oakland police responded shortly before 1:30 a.m. to multiple ShotSpotter activations in the 2000 block of International Boulevard. When officers arrived, they found an adult man suffering from apparent gunshot wounds. Officers attempted life-saving measures before the man was taken to a hospital, where he later died. The Oakland Police Department’s Homicide Section is investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. No additional information was immediately available. Anyone with information, video or photos related to the case is asked to contact OPD’s Homicide Section at 510-238-3821, the Tip Line at 510-238-7950 or email cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

headlines.title: More Oakland residents say city is headed in right direction, survey finds
headlines.description: A new survey shows more Oakland residents believe their city is headed in the right direction, though concerns remain. According to the annual Pulse Survey released Wednesday by the Oakland Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, more Oakland residents believe the city is headed in the right direction than the wrong direction for the first time since 2017. The findings are based on interviews with 720 Oakland residents conducted over a nine-day period that ended Sunday. 46% said Oakland is headed in the right direction, while 36% said it’s headed in the wrong direction. For comparison, in 2024, only 12% said the city was headed in the right direction, compared to the 75% that said it was headed the wrong direction. NBC Bay Area’s Bob Redell has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Thousands of California state workers walk off job in one-day strike
headlines.description: Thousands of state workers have walked off the job in a one-day strike that is expected to be felt across the Bay Area. SEIU Local 1000 puts the number of workers on strike at about 95,000. The workers serve in more than 140 state departments and agencies, including the DMV and state benefits programs such as disability and unemployment. The strike is happening statewide and for the first time in the union’s history. In the Bay Area, there are two locations where workers will be on the picket lines: outside the California Public Utilities Commission in San Francisco and at the Elihu Harris State Building in Oakland. SEIU Local 1000 is the largest public-sector union in the state and one of the largest in the country. The one-day strike comes after failed negotiations between workers and Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejer Saab has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: San Jose begins installing new speed cameras
headlines.description: San Jose has installed new speed cameras throughout the city to keep streets safer. Over the weekend, crews began installing automated speed enforcement cameras as part of a five-year pilot program authorized under a new California state law. A total of 33 new speed cameras will be up when the project is completed. San Jose has recorded 41 traffic deaths this year. City leaders hope the cameras will help save lives. The program has already launched in Oakland and San Francisco. In San Francisco, the city says dangerous speeding dropped by 84% at camera locations during the first 18 months of enforcement. Numbers also show that San Francisco had roughly 40,000 fewer cases of speeding every day across camera locations. Editor’s note: A previous version of this story inaccurately reported all 33 speed cameras have been installed.
